newsitem.title: INDIA: India talks seek more women in world parliaments.
newsitem.headline: India talks seek more women in world parliaments.

text.p: An international conference of parliamentarians on Tuesday called for a substantial increase in the number of women in national politics.

"Nearly all delegates stated that the constitutions of their countries provided equality between men and women in all spheres of life," said Purno Sangma, president of the conference organised by the Geneva-based Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU).

"However, all those who spoke affirmed that in politics there was a huge gap between law and practice with regard to the principle of equality," said Sangma, who is speaker of India's lower house of parliament.
The IPU organised the 77-nation meeting, which ended on Tuesday, as a follow-up to the United Nations Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995.
"The situation would improve appreciably if the number of women in parliament reached a certain threshold figure," Sangma said.
"This critical mass was evaluated at 30 percent which has also been borne out by the experience of the Nordic countries," Sangma said.
The conference called for the private sector to step in to correct a social bias that has so far stirred only activists.

"Without the inclusion of women in decision-making, real development cannot in fact take place, and cooperation and understanding between the sexes will remain a pipe dream," Namibian President Sam Nujoma told the conference on Saturday.
Some 250 lawmakers from across the world took part in the conference.
Among other issues, delegates at the conference discussed financing electoral campaigns and job quotas for women in legislatures.
United Nations assistant secretary-general Angela King told the meeting that women were consistently under-represented in power structures all over the world.
The IPU said last week that the share of women among parliamentarians had dropped to 11.7 percent from a high of 14.6 percent in 1988.
The group, which surveyed 1,000 political parties and 179 parliaments worldwide, said only one out of 10 party leaders was a woman despite a large number of female activists.
Only six nations -- Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, North Korea, Nepal and the Philippines -- had laws requiring national legislatures to include a minimum percentage of women, the IPU study said.
Even in these nations, the share of women in parliaments was far below the proportion of women in the population, it said.
